JAMA Neurology

Delirium and Long-Term Cognitive Trajectories in Cognitively Unimpaired Adults

Palmer AK, Mullan AF, Graff-Radford J et al. · 2026 Nov 02
Study Type: Prospective population-based cohort study (Mayo Clinic Study of Aging, US), with delirium modelled as a time-dependent exposure.
Key Question: Is in-hospital delirium associated with subsequent MCI, dementia and cognitive decline in adults who were not demented at baseline?
Key Findings:
  • Of 3501 hospitalised participants (median age 74.1 years), 75 (2.1%) had delirium documented, identified by NLP of clinical notes.
  • Delirium was associated with incident MCI (aHR 3.67; 95% CI 2.19–6.15) and dementia (aHR 5.39; 95% CI 2.94–9.85), adjusted for age, sex, education and APOE ε4 status.
  • Delirium was also associated with accelerated decline on longitudinal cognitive testing (effect sizes not reported in abstract).
Clinical Relevance: Supports delirium prevention and structured post-delirium cognitive follow-up in older NHS inpatients, who may be at substantially elevated risk of later cognitive impairment.
Limitations: Delirium was rare (2.1%) and NLP-derived, which likely means under-ascertainment and a small exposed group; residual confounding by illness severity, frailty and pre-existing subclinical neurodegeneration cannot be excluded.

Neurology

Impact of 2024 Revisions of Multiple Sclerosis Diagnostic Criteria in People With Radiologically Isolated Syndrome

Di Filippo M, Masillo V, Di Sabatino E et al. · 2026 Dec 08
Study Type: Multicentre retrospective registry-based cohort study (22 Italian tertiary MS centres; n=236).
Key Question: What proportion of people with radiologically isolated syndrome (RIS) would be reclassified as MS under the 2024 McDonald criteria?
Key Findings:
  • At baseline, 159/236 (67.4%) met 2024 MS criteria, largely driven by DIS (96.6%) plus CSF positivity (75.6% of those tested); radiologic DIT was present in only 21.6%.
  • Among 42 who later had a clinical event, 88.1% would have been diagnosed with MS a median of 2 years (IQR 1.0–5.5) earlier. A further 18 (7.6%) qualified through new radiologic DIT during follow-up (median 3.0 years).
  • CVS data were available for only 5 patients (none positive), so its contribution could not be assessed.
Clinical Relevance: Most people currently labelled RIS could be diagnosed with MS before any clinical event, prompting UK services to consider how this affects incidental-finding pathways, CSF use, and early treatment decisions.
Limitations: The retrospective, real-world design with non-standardised MRI, incomplete CSF/kappa free light chain data and negligible CVS assessment, and no outcome data showing that earlier diagnosis improves prognosis.

Annals of Neurology

Understanding the Pattern of Cognitive Decline in GBA1-Related Parkinson's Disease: An Exploratory Longitudinal Multi-Cohort Study

Bode M, Pauly C, Jónsdóttir SR et al. · 2026 Nov 02
Study Type: Exploratory longitudinal multicohort study (PPMI, ABC-PD, NCER-PD); 546 controls, 903 PD without GBA1 variant, 211 PD with pathogenic GBA1 variant.
Key Question: What is the pattern, trajectory and timing of cognitive decline across domains in GBA1-related PD compared with non-carrier PD?
Key Findings:
  • GBA1 carriers performed worse at baseline in executive function, attention, visuocognitive skills and memory, with faster and more widespread decline across these domains.
  • Risk of clinically relevant impairment (test z ≤ -1.5; MoCA < 26) was higher in carriers; processing speed and visuoperceptual deficits emerged 1.2 and 2.5 disease years earlier than in non-carriers.
  • A rapidly declining subgroup within carriers was associated with male sex, depressive symptoms and severe GBA1 variants. Effect sizes and confidence intervals are not given in the abstract.
Clinical Relevance: Supports earlier and broader cognitive surveillance, including mood assessment, in GBA1-positive PD, which is relevant to UK genetic testing and trial-eligibility discussions.
Limitations: Exploratory design with heterogeneous cohorts and variable, sometimes short, follow-up limits causal inference and generalisability.

Neurology

Plasma P-Tau217 and NfL Longitudinal Changes Across Neurodegenerative Diseases: Impact of α-Synuclein in Alzheimer Disease

Esteller-Gauxax D, Pérez-Millan A, Sarto J et al. · 2026 Nov 24
Study Type: Prospective single-centre cohort study (memory clinic, Barcelona; n=223; 36-month follow-up).
Key Question: How do plasma p-tau217 and NfL change over 36 months across AD, DLB, FTD and non-neurodegenerative cognitive impairment, and does co-existing α-synuclein pathology (seed amplification assay-positive) modify AD trajectories?
Key Findings:
  • AD with α-synuclein co-pathology (AD-aSyn+, n=15) had the steepest p-tau217 rise (2.19 pg/mL; p<0.001); AD-aSyn- and DLB-AD+ rose less, while DLB-AD-, FTD and NNCI remained stable.
  • NfL was highest in FTD and AD-aSyn+ at baseline and follow-up (both p<0.001), with similar increases in both groups; other groups showed moderate or minimal change.
  • Baseline p-tau217 was highest in both AD groups, intermediate in DLB-AD+, and lowest in DLB-AD-, FTD and NNCI.
Clinical Relevance: α-synuclein co-pathology may identify AD patients with faster biomarker progression, relevant to prognostication and trial enrichment as plasma biomarkers move towards NHS use.
Limitations: Small subgroups (AD-aSyn+ n=15, DLB groups 13–17) from a single centre limit precision and generalisability; clinical outcomes were not reported in the abstract.

Neurology

Association of LATE-NC With Neuropathologic Lesions and Cognitive Abilities: A Population-Based Autopsy Study

Matos Silva C, Justo AFO, Ribeiro Paes V et al. · 2026 Dec 08
Study Type: Cross-sectional population-based autopsy study (n=1,860; Brazilian biobank, 2004–2024)
Key Question: How is LATE-NC associated with coexisting neuropathology and cognition in an ethnoracially and socioeconomically diverse, non-high-income-country sample?
Key Findings:
  • LATE-NC was present in 7.4% (stage 1: 3.0%; stage 2: 4.0%; stage 3: 0.4%).
  • Stage 2–3 LATE-NC was associated with hippocampal sclerosis (OR 14.95; 95% CI 7.42–30.27), advanced Braak NFT stage (OR 2.23; 1.32–3.83) and Lewy body pathology (OR 1.89; 1.02–3.37).
  • After adjustment for other pathologies, LATE-NC was associated with higher CDR-SOB (β=4.06; 95% CI 2.95–5.18), comparable to moderate/severe ADNC (β=3.78).
Clinical Relevance: LATE-NC contributes substantially to cognitive impairment independent of Alzheimer pathology and is likely underrecognised clinically, which is relevant when interpreting atypical amnestic dementia and biomarker-negative or mixed-pathology presentations in UK memory services.
Limitations: Cross-sectional design precludes causal inference, and few advanced-stage cases produced wide confidence intervals.

Brain

Cell-specific transcription dysregulation in human Huntington's disease-positive developing striatum

Precious SV, Bartley OJM, Linehan P et al. · 2026 Nov 04
Study Type: Exploratory single-cell RNA sequencing study (n=1 HD-positive vs n=1 control fetal striatum), with comparison to public adult postmortem HD datasets.
Key Question: Are transcriptional abnormalities already present in the developing human HD-positive striatum, and do they resemble those seen in adult HD brain?
Key Findings:
  • 2,032 differentially expressed genes were identified between HD-positive (CAG 49) and control fetal striatum, across nine cell clusters, with pathway-level dysregulation varying by cluster.
  • Fetal and adult HD striatal profiles showed substantial overlap in expression changes, though not universally; some changes were reversed.
  • No effect sizes, confidence intervals or specific affected pathways are reported in the abstract.
Clinical Relevance: Supports a neurodevelopmental component to HD, which may inform the timing and design of future disease-modifying and presymptomatic intervention trials, including for UK gene-carrier cohorts.
Limitations: A single HD and single control sample precludes any estimate of inter-individual variability, so findings are hypothesis-generating only.

Brain

Dysregulated CSF T-cell responses and their evolution after intravenous immunoglobulin in Guillain-Barré syndrome

Morrison AH, Yao T, Isfort MC et al. · 2026 Nov 05
Study Type: Prospective observational cohort study (single-cell RNA and TCR sequencing; exploratory, mechanistic)
Key Question: How do T-cell phenotype, clonality and compartmentalisation differ between blood and CSF in treatment-naïve GBS, and how are they altered by IVIg?
Key Findings:
  • Compared with healthy controls, GBS showed greater CSF-to-blood enrichment of Th1 CD4+ cells, activated effector-memory CD8+ cells and inflammatory macrophages, without increased overall T-cell clonal expansion.
  • Post-IVIg, blood changed minimally, but CSF showed reduced Th1/activated effector-memory states, increased Th2 and regulatory T cells, and altered clonal repertoire.
  • Expanded clonotypes with predicted pathogen specificity were found in six patients, and convergent clonotype groups were seen within and across patients.
Clinical Relevance: Findings support a CSF-compartmentalised pro-inflammatory T-cell mechanism in GBS and suggest IVIg acts centrally rather than peripherally, which may inform future biomarker and therapeutic work.
Limitations: Very small sample (8 pre-treatment CSF, only 3 post-treatment CSF samples), no untreated comparator for the longitudinal changes, and use of historical healthy control datasets, so treatment-effect findings are hypothesis-generating only.

Brain

Network disruption in post-stroke depressive symptoms: a Bayesian multicohort study

Klingbeil J, Wawrzyniak M, Tourdias T et al. · 2026 Nov 06
Study Type: Multicohort retrospective reanalysis of four observational cohorts (n=1,864) using Bayesian voxel-wise lesion mapping, structural disconnection and functional lesion network mapping (normative connectome data).
Key Question: Which lesion locations and network disruptions are associated with post-stroke depressive symptoms, and where is there evidence against an association?
Key Findings:
  • Lesion associations clustered in the right hemisphere (frontal, insular, parietal cortex; striatum, amygdala, hippocampus; adjacent white matter), with Bayesian evidence of *no* association across large left-hemisphere areas.
  • Structural disconnection was associated with symptoms in bilateral frontal white matter, notably the corpus callosum and anterior thalamic radiation; strongest overall signal was right frontal lesions and right-dominant frontal cortico-subcortical disconnection.
  • Functional lesion network mapping implicated left posterior cingulate/precuneus, and less consistently bilateral anterior insula. Effect sizes and Bayes factors were not reported in the abstract.
Clinical Relevance: Lesion location and network disruption may help identify patients at higher risk of post-stroke depression for earlier screening, though this is not yet actionable in NHS stroke pathways.
Limitations: Retrospective analysis of heterogeneous cohorts using normative rather than individual connectomes, with no prospective validation or predictive performance data reported.
